articles.title: Double dual of a lattice over a Dedekind domain
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain with
fraction field $K$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module
through $A \subseteq K$, and let $B$ be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on $V$. For an
$A$-submodule $N$ of $V$ write $N^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in N\}$.
If $M$ is an $A$-lattice in $V$, that is, a finitely generated $A$-submodule that spans $V$ over
$K$, then $(M^\vee)^\vee = M$.

No reflexivity hypothesis on $M$ is needed: over a Dedekind domain a finitely generated
torsion-free module is flat, hence projective, hence reflexive.

## Sources

- ATLAS NumberTheoryI, Proposition 5.16.

articles.title: The dual of a lattice is finitely generated
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Noetherian integral domain with
fraction field $K$, let $V$ be a $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module through
$A \subseteq K$, and let $B$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$. Let $M$ be a finitely
generated $A$-submodule of $V$ that spans $V$ over $K$. Then the dual submodule
$M^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M\}$ is a finitely generated
$A$-submodule of $V$.

articles.title: Double dual of a reflexive lattice
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an integral domain with fraction field $K$,
let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module through $A \subseteq K$,
and let $B$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$. Let $M$ be an $A$-lattice in $V$, that is, a
finitely generated $A$-submodule that spans $V$ over $K$, and suppose that $M$ is reflexive as an
$A$-module. Let $M^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M\}$. Then
$\{x \in V : B(y, x) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M^\vee\} = M$.

This is the lattice analogue of the corresponding statement for the $A$-span of a $K$-basis of
$V$: no basis is needed when $M$ is reflexive as an $A$-module.

articles.title: The dual lattice and the dual module
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Noetherian integral domain with
fraction field $K$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module
through $A \subseteq K$, and let $B$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$. Let $M$ be an
$A$-lattice in $V$, that is, a finitely generated $A$-submodule that spans $V$ over $K$, and let
$M^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M\}$. Then $M^\vee$ is an $A$-lattice
in $V$, and the map $M^\vee \to \operatorname{Hom}_A(M, A)$ sending $x$ to the functional
$y \mapsto B(x, y)$ is bijective.

articles.title: The dual of a lattice is a lattice
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a Noetherian integral domain with fraction
field $K$, let $V$ be a $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module through $A \subseteq K$, and let
$B$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$. If $M$ is an $A$-lattice in $V$, that is, a finitely
generated $A$-submodule that spans $V$ over $K$, then so is its dual submodule
$M^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M\}$.

articles.title: The dual submodule is the dual module
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an integral domain with fraction field
$K$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module through
$A \subseteq K$, let $B$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$, and let $M$ be an $A$-submodule
of $V$ that spans $V$ over $K$. Write
$M^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M\}$. This is the isomorphism of
$A$-modules $M^\vee \cong \operatorname{Hom}_A(M, A)$ that sends $x$ to the functional
$y \mapsto B(x, y)$.

articles.title: The dual of a finitely generated submodule spans
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with
fraction field $K$, let $V$ be a $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module through $A \to K$, and
let $B$ be a bilinear form on $V$. If $M$ is a finitely generated $A$-submodule of $V$, then its
dual submodule $M^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M\}$ spans $V$ over
$K$.

articles.title: Dual submodules commute with localization
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an integral domain with fraction
field $K$, let $V$ be a $K$-vector space that is also an $A$-module compatibly with $A \to K$, and
let $B$ be a $K$-bilinear form on $V$. For a subring $R \subseteq K$ and an $R$-submodule $N$ of
$V$, write $N^\vee_R = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in R \text{ for all } y \in N\}$ for the dual of $N$
over $R$. Let $S$ be a submonoid of $A$ consisting of non-zero-divisors, and let
$A_S = \{a/s : a \in A,\ s \in S\} \subseteq K$ be the localization of $A$ at $S$. Then for every
finitely generated $A$-submodule $M$ of $V$, the dual over $A_S$ of the $A_S$-span of $M$ equals
the $A_S$-span of the dual $M^\vee_A$ of $M$ over $A$.

articles.title: Bijectivity of the dual pairing
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an integral domain with fraction field $K$,
let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module through $A \subseteq K$,
let $B$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$, and let $M$ be an $A$-submodule of $V$ that
spans $V$ over $K$. Then the map from
$M^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M\}$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M, A)$
sending $x$ to the functional $y \mapsto B(x, y)$ is bijective.

articles.title: Surjectivity of the dual pairing
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be an integral domain with fraction field $K$,
let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module through $A \subseteq K$,
let $B$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form on $V$, and let $M$ be an $A$-submodule of $V$ that
spans $V$ over $K$. Then the map from
$M^\vee = \{x \in V : B(x, y) \in A \text{ for all } y \in M\}$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_A(M, A)$
sending $x$ to the functional $y \mapsto B(x, y)$ is surjective.

articles.title: A spanning submodule localizes to the whole space
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring with
fraction field $K$, let $V$ be a $K$-vector space, viewed as an $A$-module through $A \to K$, and
let $M$ be an $A$-submodule of $V$ that spans $V$ over $K$. Then $V$, together with the inclusion
$M \hookrightarrow V$, is the localization of the $A$-module $M$ at the non-zero-divisors of $A$.

Concretely, every non-zero-divisor $s$ of $A$ acts bijectively on $V$, and every $v \in V$
satisfies $s v \in M$ for some non-zero-divisor $s$ of $A$.

articles.title: The $p$-neighbor relation is symmetric
articles.statement:
For every natural number $p$ and all submodules
$L_1$, $L_2$ of a module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are $p$-neighbors if
and only if $L_2$ and $L_1$ are $p$-neighbors.

articles.title: $p$-neighbors of submodules
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-module and $p$ a
natural number. Two submodules $L_1$ and $L_2$ of $M$ are $p$-neighbors when $p$ is prime and the
intersection $L_1 \cap L_2$ has index $p$ in each of them, that is, the quotients
$L_1 / (L_1 \cap L_2)$ and $L_2 / (L_1 \cap L_2)$ both have exactly $p$ elements.

articles.title: No submodules are $1$-neighbors
articles.statement:
For any submodules $L_1$ and $L_2$ of a module $M$
over a commutative ring $R$, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are not $1$-neighbors, since $1$ is not prime.

articles.title: Dual submodule of an orthogonal product
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $S$ be a
field that is an $R$-algebra, and let $M_1$, $M_2$ be vector spaces over $S$ that are also
$R$-modules compatibly with $R \to S$. For a bilinear form $B$ over $S$ on such a space $M$ and an
$R$-submodule $N$ of $M$, the dual of $N$ is
$N^\vee = \{x \in M : B(x, y) \in R \text{ for all } y \in N\}$, where $R$ stands for its image
in $S$. Let $B_1$, $B_2$ be bilinear forms over $S$ on $M_1$, $M_2$, and let $B_1 \oplus B_2$ be
their orthogonal product on $M_1 \times M_2$, given by
$(B_1 \oplus B_2)((x_1, x_2), (y_1, y_2)) = B_1(x_1, y_1) + B_2(x_2, y_2)$. Then for all
$R$-submodules $N_1 \subseteq M_1$ and $N_2 \subseteq M_2$, the dual of $N_1 \times N_2$ with
respect to $B_1 \oplus B_2$ is $N_1^\vee \times N_2^\vee$, where $N_1^\vee$ and $N_2^\vee$ are
taken with respect to $B_1$ and $B_2$.

articles.title: Nondegeneracy of an orthogonal product
articles.statement:
Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ be bilinear forms on modules
$M_1$ and $M_2$ over a commutative semiring $R$. Their orthogonal product $B_1 \oplus B_2$ on
$M_1 \times M_2$ is nondegenerate (both left- and right-separating) if and only if $B_1$ and
$B_2$ are both nondegenerate.

articles.title: Evaluation of an orthogonal product
articles.statement:
Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ be bilinear forms on modules
$M_1$ and $M_2$ over a commutative semiring $R$, with orthogonal product $B_1 \oplus B_2$ on
$M_1 \times M_2$. For all $x = (x_1, x_2)$ and $y = (y_1, y_2)$ in $M_1 \times M_2$,
$(B_1 \oplus B_2)(x, y) = B_1(x_1, y_1) + B_2(x_2, y_2)$.

articles.title: Orthogonal product of bilinear forms
articles.statement:
Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ be bilinear forms on modules
$M_1$ and $M_2$ over a commutative semiring $R$. Their orthogonal product $B_1 \oplus B_2$ is the
bilinear form on $M_1 \times M_2$ given by
$(B_1 \oplus B_2)((x_1, x_2), (y_1, y_2)) = B_1(x_1, y_1) + B_2(x_2, y_2)$.

articles.title: Basis independence of the rank of a bilinear form
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field
$K$, let $B$ be a bilinear form on $V$, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in n_1}$ and
$c = (c_j)_{j \in n_2}$ be bases of $V$ indexed by finite types $n_1$ and $n_2$. Then the rank of
$B$ with respect to $b$ equals the rank of the Gram matrix $(B(c_i, c_j))_{i, j \in n_2}$ of $B$
in $c$.

Proof: The Gram matrix in one basis is the Gram matrix in the other multiplied on both sides by
change-of-basis matrices. Since the rank of a product is at most the rank of each factor, each
rank is at most the other, hence they are equal.

## Sources

- N. Bourbaki, Algebra I, Chapters 1-3, Springer (1989), Chapter III.

articles.title: Rank of a bilinear form via its Gram matrix
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $K$, let
$B$ be a bilinear form on $V$, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in n}$ be a basis of $V$ indexed by a finite
type $n$. Then the rank of $B$ with respect to $b$ equals the rank of the Gram matrix
$(B(b_i, b_j))_{i, j \in n}$. This holds by definition.

## Sources

- N. Bourbaki, Algebra I, Chapters 1-3, Springer (1989), Chapter III.

articles.title: Rank of a bilinear form
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $K$, let $B$ be a bilinear
form on $V$, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in n}$ be a basis of $V$ indexed by a finite type $n$. The
rank of $B$ with respect to $b$ is the rank of the Gram matrix $(B(b_i, b_j))_{i, j \in n}$ of $B$
in $b$.

By the basis independence theorem, this number does not depend on the choice of $b$.

## Sources

- N. Bourbaki, Algebra I, Chapters 1-3, Springer (1989), Chapter III.

articles.title: The Gram matrices of a bilinear form in two bases have the same rank
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector
space over a field $K$, let $B$ be a bilinear form on $V$, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in n_1}$ and
$c = (c_j)_{j \in n_2}$ be bases of $V$ indexed by finite types $n_1$ and $n_2$. Then the Gram
matrices $(B(b_i, b_j))_{i, j \in n_1}$ and $(B(c_i, c_j))_{i, j \in n_2}$ have the same rank.

articles.title: Positive-definite matrices are congruent to the identity
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a real square matrix
with rows and columns indexed by a finite set, and suppose $P$ is positive definite: $P$ is
symmetric and $x^{\mathsf{T}} P x > 0$ for every nonzero real vector $x$. Then there is an
invertible real matrix $Q$ of the same size such that $Q^{\mathsf{T}} P Q = I$, where $I$ is the
identity matrix.

articles.title: Simultaneous diagonalization by congruence
articles.statement:
Let $S$ and $P$ be real square matrices with rows
and columns indexed by a finite set $n$, where $S$ is symmetric and $P$ is positive definite. Then
there is an invertible real matrix $C$, indexed by $n$, such that $C^{\mathsf T} S C$ is diagonal
and $C^{\mathsf T} P C$ is the identity matrix.

Proof: Normalize $P$ to the identity by a congruence built from its orthonormal eigenbasis, scaled
by the inverse square roots of its eigenvalues, then orthogonally diagonalize the transformed
symmetric matrix. This is the argument of Wikipedia's "Definite matrix", section "Simultaneous
diagonalization", with the eigenbasis scaling in place of a Cholesky factor.

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Theorem 4.5.15.

articles.title: Sylvester's law of inertia
articles.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be real symmetric square matrices with rows
and columns indexed by a finite set $n$, and suppose $B = P^{\mathsf T} A P$ for some invertible
real matrix $P$ indexed by $n$. Then $A$ and $B$ have the same number of positive eigenvalues, the
same number of negative eigenvalues and the same number of zero eigenvalues, each counted with
multiplicity.

Proof: By the spectral theorem, the quadratic form of each matrix is a weighted sum of squares
whose weights are its eigenvalues. Congruence gives an equivalence of quadratic forms, and
invariance of the signature fixes the positive and negative counts; the zero count follows by
trichotomy.

## Sources

- J. J. Sylvester, *A demonstration of the theorem that every homogeneous quadratic polynomial is reducible by real orthogonal substitutions to the form of a sum of positive and negative squares*, Philosophical Magazine Ser. 4, 4(23) (1852), 138-142.

articles.title: Evaluating an orthogonal sum of systems of quadratic forms
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
semiring, let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules, and let $(Q_i)_{i \in \iota}$ and
$(Q'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be families of quadratic forms on $M$ and on $N$ indexed by the same
type $\iota$. For every index $i$ and every $(x, y) \in M \times N$, the $i$-th form of their
pointwise orthogonal sum takes the value $Q_i(x) + Q'_i(y)$ at $(x, y)$.

articles.title: Orthogonal sum of systems on the left summand
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring,
let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules, and let $(Q_i)_{i \in \iota}$ and $(Q'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be
families of quadratic forms on $M$ and on $N$ indexed by the same type $\iota$. For every
index $i$ and every $x \in M$, the $i$-th form of their pointwise orthogonal sum takes the
value $Q_i(x)$ at $(x, 0) \in M \times N$.

articles.title: Orthogonal sum of systems on the right summand
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring,
let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules, and let $(Q_i)_{i \in \iota}$ and $(Q'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be
families of quadratic forms on $M$ and on $N$ indexed by the same type $\iota$. For every
index $i$ and every $y \in N$, the $i$-th form of their pointwise orthogonal sum takes the
value $Q'_i(y)$ at $(0, y) \in M \times N$.

articles.title: Orthogonal sum of systems of quadratic forms
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative semiring, let
$M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules, and let $(Q_i)_{i \in \iota}$ and $(Q'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be families
of quadratic forms on $M$ and on $N$ indexed by the same type $\iota$. Their pointwise
orthogonal sum is the family $(Q_i \oplus Q'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of quadratic forms on
$M \times N$, where $Q_i \oplus Q'_i$ is the orthogonal sum given by
$(Q_i \oplus Q'_i)(x, y) = Q_i(x) + Q'_i(y)$.

articles.title: Carroll (Desnanot–Jacobi) identity
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n$ be a natural
number, and let $C$ be an $(n + 2) \times (n + 2)$ matrix over $R$. For indices $a$ and $b$,
write $C^{a}_{b}$ for the $(n + 1) \times (n + 1)$ matrix obtained from $C$ by deleting row $a$
and column $b$. Let $i \ne j$ be distinct indices and let $C^{ij}_{ij}$ be the $n \times n$
matrix obtained from $C$ by deleting rows $i$ and $j$ and columns $i$ and $j$. Then

$$\det C \cdot \det C^{ij}_{ij} = \det C^{i}_{i} \det C^{j}_{j} - \det C^{i}_{j} \det C^{j}_{i}.$$

For $n = 0$ the matrix $C^{ij}_{ij}$ is empty and its determinant is $1$.

## Sources

- Charles Delorme and Guillermo Pineda-Villavicencio, "Quadratic Form Representations via Generalized Continuants", Journal of Integer Sequences 18 (2015), Article 15.6.4, displayed lemma lines 133–142. https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL18/Pineda/pin2.tex. The source cites C. L. Dodgson, "Condensation of determinants, being a new and brief method for computing their arithmetical values", Proc. Roy. Soc. Lond. 15 (1866), 150–155.

articles.title: Binomial entry bound for bit-swap pieces
articles.statement: Each entry of the `i`th piece is bounded by the number of `i`-subsets of the bit positions.

articles.title: Uniform power-of-two entry bound for bit-swap pieces
articles.statement: The uniform entry bound used in the source: every piece has absolute value at most `2 ^ n`.

articles.title: Antisymmetric two-bit singlet vector
articles.statement: The unnormalized antisymmetric two-bit vector, in order `00, 01, 10, 11`.

articles.title: One-bit swap matrix as identity minus singlet outer product
articles.statement: The one-bit swap matrix is the identity minus the singlet outer product.

articles.title: Bit-swap pieces vanish beyond the number of bits
articles.statement: There is no piece containing more antisymmetric factors than bit positions.

articles.title: Piece of an n-bit swap with i antisymmetric factors
articles.statement: The part of an `n`-bit swap with exactly `i` antisymmetric factors.

articles.title: Bit-swap pieces sum to the swap permutation matrix
articles.statement: The `n + 1` grouped pieces sum to the permutation matrix swapping the two bit strings.

articles.title: The coefficient of $X$ in $\det(B + XA)$
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ and
$B$ be square matrices over $R$ indexed by a finite type $n$. Regard $B + XA$ as a matrix over
the polynomial ring $R[X]$. Then the coefficient of $X$ in the polynomial $\det(B + XA)$ equals
the first-order term of the determinant $L_B(A) = \sum_{i \in n} \det B^{(i)}$, where $B^{(i)}$
is the matrix $B$ with its $i$-th row replaced by the $i$-th row of $A$.

articles.title: The determinant is affine along a rank-one direction
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $B$ be a
square matrix over $K$ indexed by a finite type $n$, and let $u, v \in K^n$. Then for every
$t \in K$, $\det(B + t\,uv^{\mathsf T}) = \det B + t\,(\det(B + uv^{\mathsf T}) - \det B)$.

articles.title: Additivity of the first-order term of the determinant
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring
and let $A$, $B$, $C$ be square matrices over $R$ indexed by a finite type $n$. Write
$L_B(A) = \sum_{i \in n} \det B^{(i)}_A$, where $B^{(i)}_A$ is the matrix $B$ with its $i$-th
row replaced by the $i$-th row of $A$. Then $L_B(A + C) = L_B(A) + L_B(C)$.

articles.title: Homogeneity of the first-order term of the determinant
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring,
let $a \in R$, and let $A$ and $B$ be square matrices over $R$ indexed by a finite type $n$.
Write $L_B(A) = \sum_{i \in n} \det B^{(i)}_A$, where $B^{(i)}_A$ is the matrix $B$ with its
$i$-th row replaced by the $i$-th row of $A$. Then $L_B(aA) = a \, L_B(A)$.

articles.title: First-order term of the determinant
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $A$ and $B$ be
square matrices over $R$ indexed by a finite type $n$. The first-order term of the determinant
of $B$ in the direction $A$ is $L_B(A) = \sum_{i \in n} \det B^{(i)}$, where $B^{(i)}$ is the
matrix $B$ with its $i$-th row replaced by the $i$-th row of $A$.

It is the coefficient of $X$ in the polynomial $\det(B + XA)$.

articles.title: Generalized factorial matrices: decomposition, determinant and inverse
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $p$ be a natural number, let $x_0, \dots, x_{p-1} \in K$ be
pairwise distinct, and let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{R}$. For $y \in K$,
$a \in \mathbb{R}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ write $(y \mid a)_n = \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} (y - ja)$.
Let numbers $S(a, b, c; n, k) \in K$, for $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ and $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$,
satisfy $S(a, b, c; n, k) = 0$ whenever $k > n$, and
$(y \mid a)_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} S(a, b, c; n, k)\,(y - c \mid b)_k$ for all
$a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$, $y \in K$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. For $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ let
$\mathbf{S}(a, b, c)$ be the $p \times p$ matrix with entries $S(a, b, c; i, k)$, let $G_a$
be the $p \times p$ matrix with entries $(x_k \mid a)_i$, and let $H$ be the $p \times p$
matrix with entries $(x_k - \gamma \mid \beta)_i$, where $0 \le i, k < p$. Then
$G_\alpha = \mathbf{S}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\, H$; $\det G_\alpha = \det G_0$;
$\det G_0 = \prod_{0 \le i < k < p} (x_k - x_i)$; $G_\alpha$ is invertible; and
$G_\alpha^{-1} = G_0^{-1}\, \mathbf{S}(0, \alpha, 0)$.

This holds for every $p$, including $p = 0$.

articles.title: Pan's theorem on generalized factorial matrices
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$,
let $p$ be a positive integer, let $x_0, \dots, x_{p-1} \in K$ be pairwise distinct, and let
$\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{R}$. For $y \in K$, $a \in \mathbb{R}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$
write $(y \mid a)_n = \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} (y - ja)$. Let numbers $S(a, b, c; n, k) \in K$, for
$a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ and $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$, satisfy $S(a, b, c; n, k) = 0$ whenever
$k > n$, and $(y \mid a)_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} S(a, b, c; n, k)\,(y - c \mid b)_k$ for all
$a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$, $y \in K$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. For $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ let
$\mathbf{S}(a, b, c)$ be the $p \times p$ matrix with entries $S(a, b, c; i, k)$, let $G_a$
be the $p \times p$ matrix with entries $(x_k \mid a)_i$, and let $H$ be the $p \times p$
matrix with entries $(x_k - \gamma \mid \beta)_i$, where $0 \le i, k < p$. Then
$G_\alpha = \mathbf{S}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)\, H$; $\det G_\alpha = \det G_0$;
$\det G_0 = \prod_{0 \le i < k < p} (x_k - x_i)$; $G_\alpha$ is invertible; and
$G_\alpha^{-1} = G_0^{-1}\, \mathbf{S}(0, \alpha, 0)$.

## Sources

- Jiaqiang Pan, "Matrix Decomposition of the Unified Generalized Stirling Numbers and Inversion of the Generalized Factorial Matrices," Journal of Integer Sequences 15 (2012), Article 12.6.6, Theorem, lines 428–460, https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL15/Pan/pan19.tex. It follows from `pan_vandermonde_general`; the hypothesis `hp` is unused and keeps the source's shape.

articles.title: Symmetry criterion for matrices indexed by a product
articles.statement:
A matrix on a product is symmetric exactly when its restrictions to each row and column are
symmetric and both diagonals of every ordered rectangle agree in opposite directions.

articles.title: Jacobi's formula
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a finite type, and let $A$ be a curve
$\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ of square real matrices with rows and columns indexed
by $n$. Suppose $A$ is differentiable at $t \in \mathbb{R}$. Then the derivative of
$s \mapsto \det A(s)$ at $t$ is $\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\operatorname{adj}(A(t))\, A'(t)\bigr)$,
where $\operatorname{adj}$ denotes the adjugate matrix and $A'(t)$ the derivative of $A$ at $t$.

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge Univ. Press, 2013, §0.8.10; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi%27s_formula

articles.title: Matrix determinant lemma in column-times-row form
articles.statement:
The matrix determinant lemma in the `replicateCol` / `replicateRow`
form stated in Mathlib's TODO for
`Matrix.det_add_replicateCol_mul_replicateRow`. The `_general` suffix
avoids clashing with Mathlib's invertible version of the same name.

articles.title: Multiplicative matrix determinant lemma for invertible matrices
articles.statement:
The matrix determinant lemma in multiplicative form, when `A.det` is a
unit: this recovers Mathlib's
`Matrix.det_add_replicateCol_mul_replicateRow` from the general version.

articles.title: Matrix determinant lemma without invertibility
articles.statement:
The **matrix determinant lemma**, without any invertibility hypothesis:
the determinant of a rank-one update of `A` is `det A` plus the adjugate
pairing `v ⬝ᵥ (adjugate A *ᵥ u)`. This is the general version left as a TODO
in Mathlib's `Matrix.det_add_replicateCol_mul_replicateRow`.

articles.title: Invertibility criterion for a rank-one update
articles.statement:
A rank-one update of `A` is a unit exactly when the adjugate correction
term is a unit; no invertibility hypothesis on `A` is needed.

articles.title: Intertwining passes to the exponential
articles.statement:
If `A * X = X * B` for a rectangular matrix
`X`, then `exp A * X = X * exp B`.

articles.title: Determinant of the matrix exponential
articles.statement:
For every complex square matrix $A$ indexed by a
finite set, $\det(e^A) = e^{\operatorname{tr} A}$, where $e^A$ is the matrix exponential. This
identity is sometimes called Jacobi's formula.

Proof: the three cases of B. C. Hall, An Elementary Introduction to Groups and Representations,
https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0005032, Theorem 3.10. The Jordan-Chevalley decomposition writes
$A = N + S$ with $N$ nilpotent, $S$ semisimple and $NS = SN$, so $e^A = e^N e^S$. Diagonalizing
$S$ gives $\det(e^S) = e^{\operatorname{tr} S}$. For the nilpotent part, where Hall uses a
strictly upper-triangular form, $e^N - I$ is nilpotent, so $\det(e^N) = 1$, while
$\operatorname{tr} N = 0$.

## Sources

- B. C. Hall, Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Representations, 2nd ed., Springer (2015), Proposition 2.23.

articles.title: Exponential of a nilpotent matrix
articles.statement:
If $A$ is a nilpotent complex square matrix indexed by a
finite set, then there is a natural number $m$ such that
$e^A = \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} \frac{1}{k!} A^k$, where $e^A$ is the matrix exponential.

Proof: if $A^m = 0$, every term of the exponential series from index $m$ on vanishes.

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Section 3.2.

articles.title: Symplectic matrices have determinant one
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $l$ a finite
set, $I$ the identity matrix indexed by $l$, and
$J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -I \\ I & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ the matrix over $R$ indexed by the disjoint
union $l \sqcup l$. Every square matrix $A$ over $R$ indexed by $l \sqcup l$ with
$A J A^{\mathsf{T}} = J$ satisfies $\det A = 1$.

## Sources

- Folklore (Pfaffian computation). Listed as §39 in O. Knill, Some Fundamental Theorems in Mathematics (https://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/graphgeometry/papers/fundamental.pdf). Problem `symplectic_matrix_det` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Diagonalizability from a split characteristic polynomial and a squarefree minimal polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let $A$ be a square matrix over $K$ with rows and columns indexed by a
finite type $n$. If the characteristic polynomial of $A$ splits over $K$ and the minimal
polynomial of $A$ (that is, of the linear map $x \mapsto Ax$ on $K^n$) is squarefree, then there
are matrices $P$ and $D$ over $K$ indexed by $n$, with $D$ diagonal and $P$ invertible, such that
$A = P D P^{-1}$.

Proof: A squarefree minimal polynomial makes the linear map $x \mapsto Ax$ semisimple, so it has a
basis of eigenvectors by the eigenbasis theorem for semisimple endomorphisms; conjugating by the
change-of-basis matrix from the standard basis gives the diagonal form.

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Theorem 1.3.12.

articles.title: Eigenbasis of a semisimple endomorphism with split characteristic polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional vector space over a field $K$ and let $f$ be a semisimple endomorphism of $V$
(every $f$-invariant subspace has an $f$-invariant complement) whose characteristic polynomial
splits over $K$. Then for every finite type $\iota$ with exactly $\dim_K V$ elements there are a
basis $(b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of $V$ and scalars $(\mu_i)_{i \in \iota}$ in $K$ such that each $b_i$
is an eigenvector of $f$ with eigenvalue $\mu_i$.

Proof: The minimal polynomial is squarefree and splits, so it is a product of distinct factors
$X - \mu$. The kernels lemma for these factors, proved by induction from the two-factor case,
shows that the eigenspaces span $V$, and bases of the eigenspaces are collected and reindexed.
This is the diagonalizability criterion derived from the kernels lemma in the French Wikipedia
article *Lemme des noyaux*, <https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemme_des_noyaux>.

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Theorem 1.3.12.

articles.title: Hermitian matrices have real-rooted characteristic polynomials
articles.statement:
The characteristic
polynomial of a Hermitian complex matrix is real-rooted.

articles.title: Spectral norm of a positive semidefinite matrix
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a positive semidefinite
complex square matrix indexed by a nonempty finite set. Then the operator norm of $A$ with
respect to the Euclidean ($\ell^2$) norm equals the largest real part of a root of the
characteristic polynomial of $A$. Since these roots are real, this is its largest root.

articles.title: Linear equivalence of eigenspaces of fg and gf
articles.statement:
For a nonzero eigenvalue, the eigenspaces of `f ∘ₗ g` and of `g ∘ₗ f`
are linearly equivalent, via `g` in one direction.

articles.title: Eigenspaces of fg and gf are equivalent, for endomorphisms
articles.statement: The `*` form of `eigenspaceCompEquiv`, for endomorphisms of one space.

articles.title: Kernel of g meets a generalized eigenspace of fg trivially
articles.statement:
If `g x = 0` and `x` lies in the generalized `μ`-eigenspace of `f ∘ₗ g`
with `μ ≠ 0`, then `x = 0`. Indeed, on the kernel of `g` the map `f ∘ₗ g`
vanishes, so `(f ∘ₗ g - μ • 1) ^ l` acts as `(-μ) ^ l • 1` there.

articles.title: Generalized eigenspaces of fg and gf are finite-dimensional together
articles.statement:
For a nonzero scalar, the generalized eigenspaces of `f ∘ₗ g` and of
`g ∘ₗ f` are finite-dimensional together, for every exponent `k : ℕ∞`.

articles.title: Generalized eigenspaces finite-dimensional together, for endomorphisms
articles.statement: The `*` form of `finite_genEigenspace_comp_iff`.

articles.title: Generalized eigenspaces of AB and BA are finite-dimensional together
articles.statement:
The generalized eigenspaces of rectangular products in opposite orders
are finite-dimensional together for a nonzero scalar and every exponent.

articles.title: Finite-dimensionality of generalized eigenspaces of ST and TS
articles.statement:
Generalized eigenspaces of reversed bounded-operator products are
finite-dimensional together for a nonzero scalar and every exponent.

articles.title: Geometric multiplicities of fg and gf agree
articles.statement:
The geometric multiplicities of a nonzero eigenvalue of `f ∘ₗ g` and of
`g ∘ₗ f` agree.

articles.title: Geometric multiplicities of fg and gf agree, for endomorphisms
articles.statement: The `*` form of `finrank_eigenspace_comp_eq`.

articles.title: Geometric multiplicities of matrix products AB and BA agree
articles.statement:
The geometric multiplicities of a nonzero eigenvalue of `A * B` and of
`B * A` agree.

articles.title: Equal geometric multiplicities of nonzero eigenvalues of ST and TS
articles.statement:
The geometric multiplicities of a nonzero eigenvalue of `S * T` and of
`T * S` agree, for bounded operators.

articles.title: Generalized eigenspaces of fg and gf have equal dimension
articles.statement:
The generalized `μ`-eigenspaces of `f ∘ₗ g` and of `g ∘ₗ f` have equal
`Module.finrank`, for every exponent `k : ℕ∞` and every nonzero `μ`.
They are finite-dimensional together; if both are infinite-dimensional, both
finranks are zero. In finite dimension only the stabilized generalized eigenspace
(for example at exponent `⊤`) measures algebraic multiplicity.

articles.title: Generalized eigenspace dimensions agree, for endomorphisms
articles.statement: The `*` form of `finrank_genEigenspace_comp_eq`.

articles.title: Generalized eigenspaces of AB and BA have equal dimension
articles.statement:
The generalized `μ`-eigenspaces of `A * B` and of `B * A` have equal
`Module.finrank`, for every exponent `k : ℕ∞`.

articles.title: Equal dimensions of generalized eigenspaces of ST and TS
articles.statement:
The generalized `μ`-eigenspaces of `S * T` and of `T * S` have equal
`Module.finrank`, for every exponent `k : ℕ∞`, for bounded operators.

articles.title: Restriction of g to generalized eigenspaces of fg and gf
articles.statement: The restriction of `g` to the generalized `μ`-eigenspaces.

articles.title: Nonzero eigenvalues of an operator times its adjoint, in either order
articles.statement:
A nonzero scalar is an eigenvalue of `T† * T` iff it is an eigenvalue of
`T * T†`, on a Hilbert space.

articles.title: Nonzero eigenvalues of fg and gf coincide
articles.statement:
A nonzero scalar is an eigenvalue of `f ∘ₗ g` iff it is an eigenvalue of
`g ∘ₗ f`.

articles.title: Nonzero eigenvalues of fg and gf coincide, for endomorphisms
articles.statement: The `*` form of `hasEigenvalue_comp_iff`.

articles.title: Nonzero eigenvalues of matrix products AB and BA coincide
articles.statement:
A nonzero scalar is an eigenvalue of the matrix product `A * B` iff it is
an eigenvalue of `B * A`.

articles.title: Nonzero eigenvalues of ST and TS coincide
articles.statement:
A nonzero scalar is an eigenvalue of `S * T` iff it is an eigenvalue of
`T * S`, for bounded operators.

articles.title: Eigenvectors of fg map to eigenvectors of gf
articles.statement:
An eigenvector of `f ∘ₗ g` for a nonzero eigenvalue is sent by `g` to an
eigenvector of `g ∘ₗ f` for the same eigenvalue.

articles.title: Eigenvectors of fg map to eigenvectors of gf, for endomorphisms
articles.statement: The `*` form of `hasEigenvector_comp`.

articles.title: Injectivity of g on generalized eigenspaces of fg
articles.statement:
The restriction of `g` to a generalized `μ`-eigenspace with `μ ≠ 0` is
injective.

articles.title: Injectivity of g between eigenspaces of fg and gf
articles.statement:
The map `g` restricted to the eigenspaces is injective when `μ ≠ 0`: if
`g x = 0` for an eigenvector `x` of `f ∘ₗ g`, then `(f ∘ₗ g) x = 0 = μ • x`,
so `x = 0`.

articles.title: Eigenspace of fg maps into the eigenspace of gf
articles.statement:
`g` sends the `μ`-eigenspace of `f ∘ₗ g` into the `μ`-eigenspace of
`g ∘ₗ f`: if `(f ∘ₗ g) x = μ • x` then `(g ∘ₗ f) (g x) = μ • (g x)`.

articles.title: Generalized eigenspace of fg maps into that of gf
articles.statement:
`g` sends the generalized `μ`-eigenspace of `f ∘ₗ g` into the generalized
`μ`-eigenspace of `g ∘ₗ f`, for every exponent. This is the intertwining
`(g ∘ₗ f) ∘ₗ g = g ∘ₗ (f ∘ₗ g)` applied to Mathlib's
`Module.End.mapsTo_genEigenspace_of_comp`.

articles.title: Surjectivity of g between eigenspaces of fg and gf
articles.statement:
The map `g` restricted to the eigenspaces is surjective when `μ ≠ 0`: an
eigenvector `y` of `g ∘ₗ f` is the image of `μ⁻¹ • f y`.

articles.title: Spectral theorem for normal matrices
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a complex square matrix whose rows and
columns are indexed by a finite set $n$, and write $M^*$ for its conjugate transpose. If $M$ is
normal, that is, $M^* M = M M^*$, then there exist a unitary matrix $P$ indexed by $n$ (so
$P^* P = P P^* = I$) and a family of complex numbers $(d_i)_{i \in n}$ such that $P^* M P$ is
the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $d_i$.

## Sources

- AlgebraNotes, Section: The Spectral Theorem, Subsection: The Spectral Theorem, Theorem (Spectral Theorem) (normal-matrix case; the Hermitian cases are Mathlib's `Matrix.IsHermitian.spectral_theorem`).

articles.title: Generalized eigenvalues of a MAX matrix to a MIN matrix
articles.statement:
Let $n > 2$ and let
$0 < s_1 < s_2 < \dots < s_n$ be real numbers. Let $M$ be the $n \times n$ matrix with entries
$M_{ij} = \max(s_i, s_j)$, let $N$ be the $n \times n$ matrix with entries
$N_{ij} = \min(s_i, s_j)$, and put $\rho = \sqrt{s_n / s_1}$. Then, as polynomials in $X$ with
real coefficients,

$$\det(M - XN) = (-1)^n \det(N) \, (X - \rho)(X + 1)^{n-2}(X + \rho).$$

The roots of $\det(M - XN)$ are the generalized eigenvalues of $M$ to $N$.

## Sources

- Jorma K. Merikoski, Pentti Haukkanen, Antonio Sasaki, and Timo Tossavainen, *On Generalized Eigenvalues of MAX Matrices to MIN Matrices and LCM Matrices to GCD Matrices*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.1, Theorem 1 (`jis-2025-25.7.1-thm-1`).

articles.title: Cauchy interlacing for generalized eigenvalues
articles.statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $A$ be a Hermitian
and $B$ a positive definite complex $(n+1) \times (n+1)$ matrix, and let $A'$ and $B'$ be their
leading principal $n \times n$ submatrices (rows and columns $1, \dots, n$). Let
$\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_{n+1}$ be real numbers such that the roots of the polynomial
$\det(A - XB)$, counted with multiplicity, are exactly $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{n+1}$, and
let $\lambda'_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda'_n$ be real numbers such that the roots of
$\det(A' - XB')$, counted with multiplicity, are exactly $\lambda'_1, \dots, \lambda'_n$. Then
$\lambda_{k+1} \le \lambda'_k \le \lambda_k$ for every $k = 1, \dots, n$.

## Sources

- Jorma K. Merikoski, Pentti Haukkanen, Antonio Sasaki, and Timo Tossavainen, *On Generalized Eigenvalues of MAX Matrices to MIN Matrices and LCM Matrices to GCD Matrices*, Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.1, Theorem 6 (`jis-2025-25.7.1-thm-6`).

articles.title: Eigenvalues of the inverse matrix
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a square matrix over a field $K$, with rows
and columns indexed by a finite type, whose determinant is a unit of $K$ (so $M$ is invertible),
and let $\mu \in K$ be nonzero. Then a vector $x$ is an eigenvector of $M$ with eigenvalue $\mu$
(that is, $x \ne 0$ and $Mx = \mu x$) if and only if $x$ is an eigenvector of $M^{-1}$ with
eigenvalue $\mu^{-1}$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigendecomposition_of_a_matrix.

articles.title: Jordan chain basis for an endomorphism with split characteristic polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be
a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $K$ and let $f$ be a linear endomorphism of $V$
whose characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $K$. Then there are
$k \in \mathbb{N}$, natural numbers $d_0, \dots, d_{k-1}$, scalars $\mu_0, \dots, \mu_{k-1} \in K$
and a basis $(b_{i,r})$ of $V$, indexed by $i < k$ and $0 \le r \le d_i$, such that
$f(b_{i,0}) = \mu_i b_{i,0}$ and $f(b_{i,j+1}) = \mu_i b_{i,j+1} + b_{i,j}$ for every $i < k$ and
every $j < d_i$, and such that the matrix of $f$ with respect to $b$ is the block-diagonal matrix
whose $i$-th diagonal block is the Jordan block of size $d_i + 1$ with eigenvalue $\mu_i$.

articles.title: Jordan chain basis for a nilpotent endomorphism
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector
space over a field $K$ and let $f$ be a nilpotent linear endomorphism of $V$. Then there are
$k \in \mathbb{N}$, natural numbers $d_0, \dots, d_{k-1}$ and a basis $(b_{i,r})$ of $V$, indexed
by $i < k$ and $0 \le r \le d_i$, such that $f(b_{i,0}) = 0$ and $f(b_{i,j+1}) = b_{i,j}$ for
every $i < k$ and every $j < d_i$, and such that the matrix of $f$ with respect to $b$ is the
block-diagonal matrix whose $i$-th diagonal block is the Jordan block of size $d_i + 1$ with
eigenvalue $0$.

articles.title: Jordan normal form
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a square matrix over a field $K$, with rows and columns indexed
by a finite set $N$, whose characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $K$. Then $A$
is similar to a block-diagonal matrix of Jordan blocks: there are $k \in \mathbb{N}$, positive
integers $s_0, \dots, s_{k-1}$, scalars $\mu_0, \dots, \mu_{k-1} \in K$, an invertible matrix $P$
with rows and columns indexed by $N$, and a bijection $e$ from the set of pairs $(i, r)$ with
$i < k$ and $r < s_i$ onto $N$, such that $A = P J P^{-1}$, where $J$ is the block-diagonal
matrix whose $i$-th diagonal block is the Jordan block of size $s_i$ with eigenvalue $\mu_i$,
with its rows and columns relabelled by $e$.

Proof: Decompose into the maximal generalized eigenspaces (Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right,
4th ed., 8.22), take a Jordan-chain basis of each nilpotent restriction, and collect them as in
the proof of Axler 8.46. The nilpotent case is proved by induction on the range, extending chains
by preimages and adding kernel vectors, as in Wikipedia, "Jordan normal form", section "A proof".

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Theorem 3.4.1.

articles.title: Entries of a Jordan block
articles.statement:
For a natural number $s$, a scalar $\mu$ in a field $K$ and indices
$i, j \in \{0, \dots, s-1\}$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the Jordan block of size $s$ with eigenvalue
$\mu$ is $1$ if $j = i + 1$, is $\mu$ if $i = j$, and is $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_normal_form.

articles.title: Jordan block
articles.statement:
For a natural number $s$ and a scalar $\mu$ in a field $K$, the Jordan block of
size $s$ with eigenvalue $\mu$ is the $s \times s$ matrix over $K$, with rows and columns indexed
by $\{0, \dots, s-1\}$, whose $(i, j)$ entry is $1$ if $j = i + 1$, $\mu$ if $i = j$, and $0$
otherwise: it has $\mu$ on the diagonal, $1$ on the first superdiagonal and $0$ elsewhere.

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Section 3.4.

articles.title: Matrix of an endomorphism on a basis of Jordan chains
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a
field $K$, let $f$ be a linear endomorphism of $V$, and let $\iota$ be a finite set. For each
$i \in \iota$ let $d_i \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\mu_i \in K$, and let $(b_{i,r})$, indexed by
$i \in \iota$ and $0 \le r \le d_i$, be a basis of $V$ such that $f(b_{i,0}) = \mu_i b_{i,0}$ and
$f(b_{i,j+1}) = \mu_i b_{i,j+1} + b_{i,j}$ for every $i \in \iota$ and every $j < d_i$. Then the
matrix of $f$ with respect to $b$ is the block-diagonal matrix whose $i$-th diagonal block is the
Jordan block of size $d_i + 1$ with eigenvalue $\mu_i$.

articles.title: Matrix of an endomorphism on a Jordan chain
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $K$,
let $f$ be a linear endomorphism of $V$, let $\mu \in K$, and let $b_0, \dots, b_d$ be a basis of
$V$ such that $f(b_0) = \mu b_0$ and $f(b_{j+1}) = \mu b_{j+1} + b_j$ for every $j < d$. Then the
matrix of $f$ with respect to the basis $(b_0, \dots, b_d)$ is the Jordan block of size $d + 1$
with eigenvalue $\mu$.

articles.title: Independence and sum of kernels of pairwise coprime polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative
ring, $M$ an $R$-module, $f$ an $R$-linear endomorphism of $M$, and $(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ a
family of polynomials in $R[X]$, indexed by a finite type $\iota$, that are pairwise coprime,
meaning that for all $i \ne j$ there are $a, b \in R[X]$ with $a p_i + b p_j = 1$. Then the
submodules $\ker p_i(f)$ are independent (each meets the sum of the others only in $0$), and
their sum is $\ker \bigl(\prod_{i \in \iota} p_i\bigr)(f)$.

articles.title: Kernel of a product of pairwise coprime polynomials
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$
an $R$-module, $f$ an $R$-linear endomorphism of $M$, and $(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ a family of
polynomials in $R[X]$ that are pairwise coprime, meaning that for all $i \ne j$ there are
$a, b \in R[X]$ with $a p_i + b p_j = 1$. Then for every finite set $s \subseteq \iota$, the sum
of the submodules $\ker p_i(f)$ over $i \in s$ equals $\ker \bigl(\prod_{i \in s} p_i\bigr)(f)$.

articles.title: Kernels lemma
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-module, $f$ an $R$-linear
endomorphism of $M$, and $(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ a family of polynomials in $R[X]$, indexed by a
finite type $\iota$, that are pairwise coprime, meaning that for all $i \ne j$ there are
$a, b \in R[X]$ with $a p_i + b p_j = 1$. Then the submodules $\ker p_i(f)$ are independent
(each meets the sum of the others only in $0$), and their sum is
$\ker \bigl(\prod_{i \in \iota} p_i\bigr)(f)$.

The decomposition is internal to $\ker \bigl(\prod_{i \in \iota} p_i\bigr)(f)$; it need not span
all of $M$.

Proof: induction on the number of polynomials from the two-polynomial case, as in the cited French
Wikipedia article. For coprime $p$ and $q$ one has $\ker p(f) + \ker q(f) = \ker (pq)(f)$, which
gives the inductive step, and independence follows because $\ker p_i(f) \cap \ker q(f) = 0$ when
$q$ is the product of the other polynomials.

## Sources

- https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemme_des_noyaux; S. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., Springer (2024), Section 8C.

articles.title: Kernels of pairwise coprime polynomials are independent over a finite set
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-module, $f$ an $R$-linear endomorphism of $M$, and
$(p_i)_{i \in \iota}$ a family of polynomials in $R[X]$ that are pairwise coprime, meaning that
for all $i \ne j$ there are $a, b \in R[X]$ with $a p_i + b p_j = 1$. Then for every finite set
$s \subseteq \iota$, every $i \in s$ and every $t \subseteq s$ with $i \notin t$, the submodule
$\ker p_i(f)$ meets the sum of the submodules $\ker p_j(f)$ over $j \in t$ only in $0$.

articles.title: Characteristic-polynomial coefficients in descending order
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a square matrix
over a commutative ring $R$ whose rows and columns are indexed by a finite set of size $N$, and
write its characteristic polynomial as $\chi_A(X) = \det(X I - A) = X^N + c_1 X^{N-1} + \dots +
c_N$. For a natural number $k$, the descending coefficient $c_k$ of $A$ is the coefficient of
$X^{N-k}$ in $\chi_A$ when $k \le N$, and $0$ when $k > N$.

Setting $c_k = 0$ for $k > N$ lets the trace recurrence be stated uniformly for all positive $k$.

articles.title: Integral of $x^r (1 - x)^r$ over $(0, 1)$
articles.statement:
For every natural number $r$ (including
$r = 0$),

$$\int_0^1 x^r (1 - x)^r \, dx = \frac{1}{(2r + 1) \binom{2r}{r}}.$$

## Sources

- Peiran Ding, Yanjun Zhu and Lei Wang, "A New Formula for the Sum of Integer Powers Based on Elementary Matrix Theory", Lemma 3.

articles.title: Newton's trace identities for the characteristic polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a square matrix
over a commutative ring $R$ whose rows and columns are indexed by a finite set of size $N$. For
each natural number $k$, let $c_k$ be the coefficient of $X^{N-k}$ in the characteristic
polynomial $\chi_A(X) = \det(X I - A)$ when $k \le N$, and $c_k = 0$ when $k > N$, so that
$\chi_A(X) = X^N + c_1 X^{N-1} + \dots + c_N$. Then for every natural number $k \ge 1$,

$$k \, c_k + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \operatorname{tr}(A^j) \, c_{k-j} = 0,$$

where $k$ is read as an element of $R$.

## Sources

- Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §220. Problem `trace_cayley_hamilton_newton` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: Traces of powers of a $2 \times 2$ matrix
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a real $2 \times 2$ matrix and
let $m \ge 1$ be an integer. Then

$$\operatorname{tr}(M^{2m}) = 2m \sum_{r=0}^{m} (-1)^r \frac{(2m - r - 1)!}{r! \, (2m - 2r)!}
(\det M)^r (\operatorname{tr} M)^{2m - 2r}$$

and

$$\operatorname{tr}(M^{2m+1}) = (2m + 1) \sum_{r=0}^{m} (-1)^r
\frac{(2m - r)!}{r! \, (2m + 1 - 2r)!} (\det M)^r (\operatorname{tr} M)^{2m + 1 - 2r}.$$

## Sources

- Peiran Ding, Yanjun Zhu and Lei Wang, "A New Formula for the Sum of Integer Powers Based on Elementary Matrix Theory", Theorem 1, equations (5) and (6).

articles.title: Smith normal form with a divisibility chain
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, let $M$
be a finitely generated free $R$-module and let $N$ be a submodule of $M$. Then there are natural
numbers $n \le m$, a basis $e_0, \dots, e_{m-1}$ of $M$, a basis $f_0, \dots, f_{n-1}$ of $N$ and
nonzero elements $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of $R$ such that $f_i = a_i e_i$ in $M$ for every $i < n$
and $a_i \mid a_{i+1}$ whenever $i + 1 < n$.

articles.title: Smith normal form
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain, let $M$ be a finitely generated free
$R$-module and let $N$ be a submodule of $M$. Then there are natural numbers $n \le m$, a basis
$e_0, \dots, e_{m-1}$ of $M$, a basis $f_0, \dots, f_{n-1}$ of $N$ and nonzero elements
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of $R$ such that $f_i = a_i e_i$ in $M$ for every $i < n$ and
$a_i \mid a_{i+1}$ whenever $i + 1 < n$.

## Sources

- H. J. S. Smith, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. 151 (1861), 293-326, DOI 10.1098/RSTL.1861.0016. It is `Submodule.exists_smith_normal_form_dvd_chain`, kept under the source's name.

articles.title: Triangularization of an endomorphism with split characteristic polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a
finite-dimensional vector space over a field $K$, let $f$ be an endomorphism of $V$ whose
characteristic polynomial splits over $K$, and let $\iota$ be a finite linearly ordered set with
exactly $\dim_K V$ elements. Then there is a basis $(b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of $V$ in which the matrix
of $f$ is upper triangular: its $(i, j)$ entry is $0$ whenever $j < i$.

Proof: induction on dimension. An eigenvector spans an invariant line, the induced map on the
quotient has split minimal polynomial (it divides that of $f$), and a triangularizing basis of the
quotient lifts, together with the eigenvector, to one of $V$. This is the eigenvector-deflation
induction of the proof of Schur's theorem in R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd
ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Theorem 2.3.1, without unitarity.

## Sources

- S. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., Springer (2024), Theorem 5.41.

articles.title: Triangularization of a matrix with split characteristic polynomial
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let
$n$ be a finite linearly ordered index set, and let $A$ be a square matrix over $K$ with rows and
columns indexed by $n$ whose characteristic polynomial splits over $K$. Then there are an
invertible matrix $P$ and a matrix $T$, both over $K$ and indexed by $n$, such that $T$ is upper
triangular ($T_{ij} = 0$ whenever $j < i$) and $A = P T P^{-1}$.

Proof: triangularize the endomorphism of $K^n$ given by $A$ in the standard basis, and conjugate
by the change-of-basis matrix from the standard basis to the triangularizing basis.

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Theorem 2.3.1.

articles.title: Evaluation of an affine function at two points
articles.statement: Evaluation of the affine function `x ↦ slope * x + intercept` at two distinct points.

articles.title: Evaluation of the dual basis
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $M$ and $N$ be
$A$-modules, let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect pairing, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$
be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$. Write $(b_i^\vee)_{i \in \iota}$ for the
dual basis of $b$ with respect to $B$, a basis of $M$. Then for all $i, j \in \iota$, the value
$B(b_i^\vee, b_j)$ equals $1$ if $j = i$ and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Dual basis with respect to a perfect pairing
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $M$
and $N$ be $A$-modules, and let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect pairing, that is, an
$A$-bilinear map such that $x \mapsto B(x, \cdot)$ is a linear isomorphism $M \to N^*$ and
$y \mapsto B(\cdot, y)$ is a linear isomorphism $N \to M^*$. Let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be
a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$, and let $(b_i^*)_{i \in \iota}$ be its dual
basis of $N^*$, where $b_i^*(b_j)$ is $1$ if $j = i$ and $0$ otherwise. The dual basis of $b$
with respect to $B$ is the basis of $M$ whose $i$-th vector is the image of $b_i^*$ under the
inverse of the isomorphism $M \to N^*$, $x \mapsto B(x, \cdot)$.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the dual basis
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $M$ and $N$ be
$A$-modules, let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect pairing, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$
be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$. If $b' = (b'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is a basis
of $M$ such that for all $i, j \in \iota$ the value $B(b'_i, b_j)$ equals $1$ if $j = i$ and
$0$ otherwise, then $b'$ is the dual basis of $b$ with respect to $B$.

articles.title: Existence of a dual basis for a perfect pairing
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $M$
and $N$ be $A$-modules, let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect pairing, and let
$b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$. Then there is a
basis $(b'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of $M$ such that for all $i, j \in \iota$ the value $B(b'_i, b_j)$
equals $1$ if $j = i$ and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Existence and uniqueness of the dual basis for a perfect pairing
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a
commutative ring, let $M$ and $N$ be $A$-modules, let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect
pairing, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$.
Then there is exactly one basis $(b'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of $M$ such that for all
$i, j \in \iota$ the value $B(b'_i, b_j)$ equals $1$ if $j = i$ and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Hom detects exact sequences ending in a surjection
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let
$M$, $N$, $P$ be $R$-modules, and let $\varphi : M \to N$ and $\psi : N \to P$ be $R$-linear
maps. Then the image of $\varphi$ equals the kernel of $\psi$ and $\psi$ is surjective if and
only if, for every $R$-module $D$ in the same universe as $N$ and $P$, precomposition with $\psi$,
$g \mapsto g \circ \psi$, is an injective map $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P, D) \to
\operatorname{Hom}_R(N, D)$ whose image is the kernel of precomposition with $\varphi$,
$h \mapsto h \circ \varphi$, as a map $\operatorname{Hom}_R(N, D) \to \operatorname{Hom}_R(M, D)$.

articles.title: Left partial trace of a rank-one matrix
articles.statement:
The partial trace of a rank-one positive semidefinite matrix is the sum
of the rank-one positive semidefinite matrices of its slices.

articles.title: Partial trace over the first factor
articles.statement: The partial trace over the first factor: `∑ i, A (i, j) (i, j')`.

articles.title: Right partial trace of a rank-one matrix
articles.statement:
The partial trace of a rank-one positive semidefinite matrix is the sum
of the rank-one positive semidefinite matrices of its slices.

articles.title: Partial trace over the second factor
articles.statement: The partial trace over the second factor: `∑ j, A (i, j) (i', j)`.

articles.title: Left partial trace preserves positive semidefiniteness
articles.statement: The partial trace over the first factor preserves positive semidefiniteness.

articles.title: Right partial trace preserves positive semidefiniteness
articles.statement: The partial trace over the second factor preserves positive semidefiniteness.

articles.title: Left partial trace is adjoint to identity amplification
articles.statement:
The partial trace over the first factor is adjoint to amplification by
the identity, in the trace pairing.

articles.title: Left partial trace of a density matrix has trace one
articles.statement: The partial trace of a density matrix has trace `1`.

articles.title: Right partial trace is adjoint to identity amplification
articles.statement:
The partial trace over the second factor is adjoint to amplification by
the identity, in the trace pairing.

articles.title: Right partial trace of a density matrix has trace one
articles.statement: The partial trace of a density matrix has trace `1`.

articles.title: Characteristic polynomial of a rank-two endomorphism
articles.statement:
The characteristic polynomial of an endomorphism of a free rank-two
module is `X² - tr f · X + det f`, the familiar quadratic formula.

articles.title: Kernel of the dual map has the same dimension as the kernel
articles.statement:
The kernel of the dual map has the same finite dimension as the kernel:
both are complementary to the range, by rank-nullity and the
dual-annihilator dimension formula.

articles.title: Trace and determinant are invariant under semiconjugacy
articles.statement:
Trace and determinant are preserved under semiconjugacy: if `e` intertwines
`f` and `g`, then `g` is the conjugate of `f` by `e`, so both invariants agree.

articles.title: Trace is additive over an invariant subspace
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space
over a field $K$, let $e$ be a linear endomorphism of $V$, and let $W$ be a subspace of $V$ with
$e(W) \subseteq W$. Then the trace of $e$ equals the trace of the restriction $e|_W$ of $e$ to $W$
plus the trace of the endomorphism $\bar e$ of the quotient $V/W$ induced by $e$:
$\operatorname{tr}(e) = \operatorname{tr}(e|_W) + \operatorname{tr}(\bar e)$.

articles.title: Trace splits along a surjective intertwining map
articles.statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector
space over a field $K$, let $W$ be a vector space over $K$, and let $q : V \to W$ be a surjective
linear map. If $f$ is a linear endomorphism of $V$ and $g$ a linear endomorphism of $W$ with
$q \circ f = g \circ q$, then $f$ maps $\ker q$ into itself, and the trace of $f$ equals the
trace of the restriction $f|_{\ker q}$ of $f$ to $\ker q$ plus the trace of $g$.

articles.title: Condition number as a singular-value ratio
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a real $n \times n$ matrix with
singular values $\sigma_0 \ge \sigma_1 \ge \dots$ on Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, indexed from
$0$ and extended by zeros, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$. If $\sigma_{n-1} \ne 0$,
then the condition number of $A$ equals $\sigma_0 / \sigma_{n-1}$.

articles.title: Infinite condition number from a vanishing singular value
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a real
$n \times n$ matrix with singular values $\sigma_0 \ge \sigma_1 \ge \dots$ on Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$, indexed from $0$ and extended by zeros, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when
$n = 0$. If $\sigma_{n-1} = 0$, then the condition number of $A$ is $\infty$.

articles.title: Condition number of the order-one identity
articles.statement:
The condition number of the $1 \times 1$
real identity matrix is $1$.

articles.title: The zero matrix has infinite condition number
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the
condition number of the real $n \times n$ zero matrix is $\infty$; this includes the
$0 \times 0$ matrix.

articles.title: Condition number of a square real matrix
articles.statement:
For a real $n \times n$ matrix $A$, let
$\sigma_0 \ge \sigma_1 \ge \dots$ be the singular values of $A$ acting on Euclidean space
$\mathbb{R}^n$, indexed from $0$ and extended by $\sigma_i = 0$ for $i \ge n$. The condition
number of $A$, an element of $[0, \infty]$, is $\infty$ if $\sigma_{n-1} = 0$ and
$\sigma_0 / \sigma_{n-1}$ otherwise, where $n - 1$ is read as $0$ when $n = 0$.

The minimum over sign matrices is only taken at positive order.

articles.title: Decay exponent of minimum sign-matrix condition numbers
articles.statement:
The decay exponent is the
supremum, taken in the extended reals $[-\infty, \infty]$, of the set of admissible exponents
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$.

The supremum need not be attained; it is $-\infty$ when no exponent is admissible.

articles.title: Adding the identity to a symmetric conference matrix gives a sign matrix
articles.statement:
If $C$ is a real
$n \times n$ symmetric conference matrix and $I$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix, then there is
a Boolean $n \times n$ matrix whose realization as a real sign matrix equals $C + I$.

articles.title: Boolean matrices realize exactly the sign matrices
articles.statement:
Send each $n \times n$ Boolean
matrix to the real matrix whose entry is $-1$ where the Boolean entry is true and $1$ where it
is false. A real $n \times n$ matrix $M$ arises in this way if and only if every entry of $M$
is $1$ or $-1$.

articles.title: Hadamard hypothesis
articles.statement:
The Hadamard hypothesis is the proposition that for every natural
number $n$ divisible by $4$ there is an $n \times n$ Hadamard matrix with integer entries, that is,
an integer matrix $H$ with all entries $\pm 1$ such that
$H H^{\mathsf{T}} = H^{\mathsf{T}} H = n I$.

This is the Hadamard conjecture, stated as a proposition to be used as a hypothesis.

articles.title: Admissible decay exponents
articles.statement:
A real number $\alpha$ is an admissible exponent when there is a
subpolynomial sequence $f \colon \mathbb{N} \to [0, \infty)$ such that for every positive integer
$n$ the minimum condition number $\kappa_n$ of the real $n \times n$ sign matrices satisfies
$\kappa_n = 1 + f(n) / n^{\alpha}$, as an equality in $[0, \infty]$.

articles.title: Subpolynomial sequences
articles.statement:
A sequence $f \colon \mathbb{N} \to [0, \infty)$ is subpolynomial
when for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ we have $f(n) = o(n^{\varepsilon})$ as $n \to \infty$.

articles.title: Symmetric conference matrices
articles.statement:
A real $n \times n$ matrix $C$ is a symmetric conference
matrix when $n \ge 2$, $C^{\mathsf{T}} = C$, every diagonal entry of $C$ is $0$, every off-diagonal
entry of $C$ is $1$ or $-1$, and $C C^{\mathsf{T}} = (n - 1) I$, where $I$ is the identity
matrix.

articles.title: The minimum condition number is attained
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$, there is an
$n \times n$ Boolean matrix whose realization as a real sign matrix ($-1$ for true, $1$ for
false) has condition number equal to the minimum condition number of order $n$.

articles.title: Minimum condition number of order one
articles.statement:
The minimum condition number of order $1$ is $1$:
the least condition number of a $1 \times 1$ real sign matrix is $1$.

articles.title: Minimum condition number of sign matrices
articles.statement:
For a positive integer $n$, the minimum
condition number of order $n$ is the least condition number of a real $n \times n$ sign matrix,
that is, a matrix all of whose entries are $1$ or $-1$; the minimum is taken over the finitely
many such matrices.

articles.title: Condition numbers are at least one
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ and every real
$n \times n$ matrix $A$, the condition number of $A$ is at least $1$.

articles.title: The minimum condition number is at least one
articles.statement:
For every positive integer $n$, the minimum
condition number of the real $n \times n$ sign matrices is at least $1$.

articles.title: Realized sign matrices have entries $\pm 1$
articles.statement:
For every Boolean $n \times n$ matrix $A$ and
all indices $i, j$, the $(i, j)$ entry of the real realization of $A$ is $1$ or $-1$.

articles.title: Real sign matrix of a Boolean matrix
articles.statement:
The realization of a Boolean $n \times n$ matrix $A$
is the real $n \times n$ matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is $-1$ if $A_{ij}$ is true and $1$ if
$A_{ij}$ is false.

articles.title: Boolean encoding of sign matrices
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, a sign matrix of order $n$ is
encoded as an $n \times n$ matrix with entries in the Booleans $\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$,
whose rows and columns are indexed by $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$.

articles.title: Spectral condition number of a positive definite matrix
articles.statement:
The spectral condition number `λ_max / λ_min` of a positive definite matrix. For `n = 0` it
is `0 / 0 = 0` (no eigenvalues), a junk value; the bound below is stated for `0 < n`.

articles.title: CG minimizes the energy norm of the error over the Krylov space
articles.statement:
For the solution `x⋆`
of `A x⋆ = b`, `‖x_k - x⋆‖_A ≤ ‖x₀ + z - x⋆‖_A` for every `z ∈ 𝒦_k(A, r₀)`.

articles.title: The conjugate gradient error bound in terms of the condition number
articles.statement:
**The conjugate gradient error bound in terms of the condition number** `κ` of `A`:
`‖x_k - x⋆‖_A ≤ 2 ((√κ - 1) / (√κ + 1))^k ‖x₀ - x⋆‖_A`.

articles.title: The conjugate gradient error bound
articles.statement:
If the eigenvalues of `A` lie in `[a, c]` with
`0 < a` and `A x⋆ = b`, the CG iterates satisfy
`‖x_k - x⋆‖_A ≤ 2 ((√κ - 1) / (√κ + 1))^k ‖x₀ - x⋆‖_A` with `κ = c / a`.

articles.title: The Chebyshev bound for Krylov energy minimizers
articles.statement:
If the eigenvalues of `A` lie in
`[a, c]` with `0 < a`, and `x` minimizes `‖· - x⋆‖_A` over `x₀ + 𝒦_k(A, A (x⋆ - x₀))`, then
`‖x - x⋆‖_A ≤ 2 ((√κ - 1) / (√κ + 1))^k ‖x₀ - x⋆‖_A` with `κ = c / a`.

articles.title: Energy norm induced by a matrix
articles.statement: The energy norm `‖v‖_A = √(vᵀ A v)`; a norm when `A` is positive definite.

articles.title: Initial conjugate gradient state
articles.statement: The initial state `x₀`, `r₀ = d₀ = b - A x₀`.

articles.title: CG stays in the Krylov space
articles.statement: `x_k - x₀ ∈ 𝒦_k(A, r₀)`.

articles.title: Conjugate gradient state after $k$ steps
articles.statement: The `k`-th conjugate gradient state from `x₀` for the system `A x = b`.

articles.title: Krylov subspace
articles.statement: The Krylov space `𝒦_k(A, r) = span {r, A r, …, A^{k-1} r}`.

articles.title: State of the conjugate gradient method
articles.statement:
The state of the conjugate gradient method: iterate `x`, residual `r = b - A x` and search
direction `d`.

articles.title: One Hestenes–Stiefel conjugate gradient step
articles.statement: One Hestenes–Stiefel conjugate gradient step.

articles.title: Schur decomposition of a complex square matrix
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a square complex matrix whose rows
and columns are indexed by a finite linearly ordered type $n$. Then there are a unitary matrix $U$,
with conjugate transpose $U^*$, and a matrix $T$ that is upper triangular with respect to the order
on $n$ (that is, $T_{ij} = 0$ whenever $j < i$) such that $A = U T U^*$.

## Sources

- I. Schur, Uber charakteristische Wurzeln, Math. Ann. 66 (1909), 488-510, DOI 10.1007/BF01450045.

articles.title: Pivot columns of a reduced row echelon matrix
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a type with elements $0$ and
$1$, and let $A$ be a matrix over $R$ in reduced row echelon form whose rows are indexed by a
linearly ordered set and whose columns are indexed by a set with a relation $<$. Suppose that the
leading entry of row $i$ of $A$ is in column $c$, that is, $A_{ic} \neq 0$ and $A_{ij} = 0$ for
every column $j < c$. Then column $c$ of $A$ is the standard basis vector $e_i$: $A_{ic} = 1$ and
$A_{kc} = 0$ for every row $k \neq i$.

articles.title: Gaussian elimination as a product of row operations
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let $A$ be a
matrix over $K$ whose rows and columns are indexed by finite linearly ordered sets. Then there
are a permutation $\sigma$ of the row indices and a finite, possibly empty, list
$M_1, \dots, M_\ell$ of square matrices over $K$ indexed by the row indices, each lower
triangular with every diagonal entry equal to $1$, such that the matrix
$M_1 M_2 \cdots M_\ell A_\sigma$ is in row echelon form. Here $A_\sigma$ is the matrix with
entries $(A_\sigma)_{ic} = A_{\sigma(i) c}$, the empty product is the identity matrix, and a
matrix $B$ is in row echelon form when for all rows $i_1 < i_2$ and every column $c$, if
$B_{i_1 c'} = 0$ for every column $c' < c$, then $B_{i_2 c} = 0$.

This records the factorization, not the intermediate matrices of an algorithm trace.

Proof: Induct on the columns after identifying the ordered index sets with initial segments of
the natural numbers; a nonzero first column uses a row pivot and recurses on the lower-right
block. Package the resulting single unit lower-triangular matrix as a one-element list (forward
elimination to row echelon form, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_elimination).

## Sources

- L. N. Trefethen and D. Bau, Numerical Linear Algebra, SIAM (1997), Lectures 20-21.

articles.title: Existence of the reduced row echelon form
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $m$ and $n$ be finite
linearly ordered sets, and let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. Then there are an
$m \times n$ matrix $R$ over $K$ in reduced row echelon form and an invertible $m \times m$
matrix $P$ over $K$ with $R = PA$. In other words, $A$ is row-equivalent to a matrix in reduced
row echelon form.

Proof: Choose pivot columns greedily (columns outside the span of the earlier ones), extend them
to a basis of $K^m$ whose order matches the order of the rows, and take $R$ to be the coordinate
matrix of the columns of $A$ in that basis and $P$ the matrix of the coordinate map.

## Sources

- G. Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 6th ed., Wellesley-Cambridge Press (2023), Section 2.2.

articles.title: Row echelon form via a row permutation and a unit lower-triangular matrix
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a
field and let $A$ be a matrix over $K$ whose rows and columns are indexed by finite linearly
ordered sets. Then there are a permutation $\sigma$ of the row indices and a square matrix $L$ over
$K$ indexed by the row indices, lower triangular with every diagonal entry equal to $1$, such that
the matrix $L A_\sigma$ is in row echelon form. Here $A_\sigma$ is the matrix with entries
$(A_\sigma)_{ic} = A_{\sigma(i) c}$, and a matrix $B$ is in row echelon form when for all rows
$i_1 < i_2$ and every column $c$, if $B_{i_1 c'} = 0$ for every column $c' < c$, then
$B_{i_2 c} = 0$.

articles.title: One pivot step of Gaussian elimination
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and let $A$ be a matrix over $K$
whose rows are indexed by a finite linearly ordered set and whose columns are indexed by any
set. Let $r$ and $i_0$ be row
indices and $j$ a column index with $A_{i_0 j} \ne 0$, and let $A'$ be the matrix obtained from
$A$ by exchanging rows $r$ and $i_0$. Then there is a square matrix $P$ over $K$ indexed by the
row indices, lower triangular with every diagonal entry equal to $1$, such that
$(P A')_{i j} = 0$ for every row $i > r$.

The row $i_0$ may be any row with a nonzero entry in column $j$; this is not
magnitude-maximizing partial pivoting.

Proof: Use an entrywise unit lower-triangular matrix whose pivot column contains the elimination
coefficients, then evaluate the matrix product as a finite sum (row operations of type 3,
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_elimination).

## Sources

- L. N. Trefethen and D. Bau, Numerical Linear Algebra, SIAM (1997), Lectures 20-21.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the reduced row echelon form
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $m$ and $n$ be finite
linearly ordered sets, and let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be $m \times n$ matrices over $K$ in reduced row
echelon form. If $R_2 = P R_1$ for some invertible $m \times m$ matrix $P$ over $K$, then
$R_1 = R_2$. In other words, a row-equivalence class contains at most one matrix in reduced row
echelon form.

Proof: Reindex the columns along the order isomorphism between $\{0, \dots, |n| - 1\}$ and $n$.
For columns indexed by an initial segment of the natural numbers, induct on the number of
columns: the matrices agree on all but the last column by induction, and that forces their last
columns to agree.

## Sources

- G. Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 6th ed., Wellesley-Cambridge Press (2023), Section 2.2.

articles.title: Invertible row operations preserve the null space
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $m$ and $n$ be
finite sets, let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$, and let $P$ be an
invertible $m \times m$ matrix over $K$. Then the linear maps $x \mapsto PAx$ and $x \mapsto Ax$
on $K^n$ have the same kernel; that is, the homogeneous systems $PAx = 0$ and $Ax = 0$ have the
same solutions.

Proof: For every $x \in K^n$ we have $(PA)x = P(Ax)$, and multiplication by $P$ is injective
because $P$ is invertible, so $(PA)x = 0$ if and only if $Ax = 0$.

## Sources

- G. Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 6th ed., Wellesley-Cambridge Press (2023), Section 2.2.

articles.title: Order-preserving reindexing of columns preserves reduced row echelon form
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a
type with elements $0$ and $1$, and let $A$ be a matrix over $R$ in reduced row echelon form whose
rows are indexed by a linearly ordered set and whose columns are indexed by a linearly ordered
set $N$. Let $e : O \to N$ be an order isomorphism from a linearly ordered set $O$. Then the
matrix $B$ with columns indexed by $O$ and entries $B_{ik} = A_{i\,e(k)}$ is in reduced row
echelon form.

articles.title: Convergence of the Jacobi method for strictly diagonally dominant matrices
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a
real square matrix with rows and columns indexed by a finite type, and let $b$ be a real vector.
Suppose $A$ is strictly diagonally dominant: $\sum_{j \ne i} |A_{ij}| < |A_{ii}|$ for every $i$.
Define the Jacobi sweep $J$ by $J(x)_i = \bigl(b_i - \sum_{j \ne i} A_{ij} x_j\bigr) / A_{ii}$.
Then there is a vector $x^*$ with $A x^* = b$ such that, for every starting vector $x_0$, the
iterates $J^k(x_0)$ converge to $x^*$ as $k \to \infty$.

## Sources

- G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins Univ. Press, 2013, §11.2; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_method

articles.title: LU decomposition without pivoting
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and $A$ an $n \times n$ matrix over
$K$ whose leading principal minors are all nonzero: for every $k \le n$, the determinant of the
upper-left $k \times k$ block of $A$ is nonzero. Then $A = LU$ for some $n \times n$ matrices
$L$ and $U$ over $K$ such that $L$ is lower triangular with every diagonal entry equal to $1$ and
$U$ is upper triangular.

Proof: Induct on the dimension and extend the factorization of the leading principal block by a
bordered (Schur-complement) step. The statement is the existence half of Wikipedia, "LU
decomposition", section "Existence and uniqueness".

## Sources

- L. N. Trefethen and D. Bau, Numerical Linear Algebra, SIAM (1997), Lecture 20.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the LU decomposition
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field and $A$ an invertible $n \times n$
matrix over $K$. Suppose $A = L_1 U_1 = L_2 U_2$, where $L_1$ and $L_2$ are lower triangular
$n \times n$ matrices over $K$ with every diagonal entry equal to $1$, and $U_1$ and $U_2$ are
upper triangular $n \times n$ matrices over $K$. Then $L_1 = L_2$ and $U_1 = U_2$.

Proof: Move the invertible triangular factors across the equality, then use the triangular inverse
and diagonal formulas to show the resulting matrix is the identity. The statement is the
uniqueness half of Wikipedia, "LU decomposition", section "Existence and uniqueness".

## Sources

- L. N. Trefethen and D. Bau, Numerical Linear Algebra, SIAM (1997), Lecture 20.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the polar decomposition of an invertible matrix
articles.statement:
Let $\mathbb{K}$ be
$\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb{K}$, indexed by a finite
type, with $\det A \neq 0$. Then there are a unitary matrix $U$ and a positive-definite matrix $P$
with $A = UP$, and they are unique: if $U'$ is unitary, $P'$ is positive definite and
$A = U'P'$, then $U' = U$ and $P' = P$.

articles.title: Polar decomposition of a complex square matrix
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a square complex matrix indexed by
a finite type, and let $A^*$ be its conjugate transpose. Then there are a unitary matrix $U$ and a
positive semidefinite matrix $P$ such that $P^2 = A^* A$ and $A = UP$.

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013).

articles.title: Polar decomposition of invertible complex matrices
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a complex square matrix with
rows and columns indexed by a finite set, and suppose $\det A \ne 0$. Then there are a unitary
matrix $U$ and a positive-definite Hermitian matrix $P$ with $A = UP$, and they are unique: if
$U'$ is unitary, $P'$ is positive-definite Hermitian and $A = U'P'$, then $U' = U$ and $P' = P$.

Proof: take $P$ to be the positive-definite square root of $A^* A$ and $U = AP^{-1}$, the
construction in Wikipedia, "Polar decomposition".

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Theorem 7.3.1.

articles.title: Polar decomposition of invertible real matrices
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a real square matrix with rows
and columns indexed by a finite set, and suppose $\det A \ne 0$. Then there are an orthogonal
matrix $O$ and a positive-definite symmetric matrix $S$ with $A = OS$, and they are unique: if
$O'$ is orthogonal, $S'$ is positive-definite symmetric and $A = O'S'$, then $O' = O$ and
$S' = S$.

Proof: take $S$ to be the positive-definite square root of $A^{\mathsf{T}} A$ and $O = AS^{-1}$,
the construction in Wikipedia, "Polar decomposition".

## Sources

- R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2013), Theorem 7.3.1.

articles.title: Rouché–Capelli theorem
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a field, let $m$ be a set and $n$ a finite set, let $A$
be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$, and let $b \in K^m$. Then the linear system $Ax = b$ has a
solution $x \in K^n$ if and only if the rank of $A$ equals the rank of the augmented matrix
$(A \mid b)$, whose columns are the columns of $A$ followed by the single column $b$.

Proof: Following the column-space argument in [Wikipedia, *Rouché–Capelli theorem*,
"Proof"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouch%C3%A9%E2%80%93Capelli_theorem#Proof), solvability is
membership of $b$ in the column span, which we compare before and after adjoining $b$.

## Sources

- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouch%C3%A9%E2%80%93Capelli_theorem.

articles.title: Singular value decomposition of a complex matrix
articles.statement:
Rectangular complex singular value decomposition: every complex `m × n` matrix
factors as `U * Σ * Vᴴ` with `U` and `V` unitary and `Σ` rectangular diagonal
with nonnegative entries; the singular values beyond the first `min m n`
(indices `j` with `m ≤ j.val`) are zero.

Proof: Apply the spectral theorem to `AᴴA`, normalize the images of the
eigenvectors with positive eigenvalues, and extend them to an orthonormal basis
of the codomain, as in the proof of S. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right,
4th ed., 7.70, and the matrix form that follows it (Section 7E).

## Sources

- S. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., Section 7E; G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins University Press (2013), Theorem 2.4.1.

articles.title: Orthogonal reduction of a real matrix to rectangular diagonal form
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a real
$m \times n$ matrix. Then there are orthogonal matrices $U$ of size $m \times m$ and $V$ of size
$n \times n$ and real numbers $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_n \ge 0$ with
$\sigma_j = 0$ for every $j > m$, such that $AV = U\Sigma$, where $\Sigma$ is the $m \times n$
matrix with $\Sigma_{jj} = \sigma_j$ for $j \le \min(m, n)$ and all other entries zero.

## Sources

- S. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., Section 7E.

articles.title: Real singular value decomposition with nonincreasing singular values
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a real
$m \times n$ matrix. Then there are orthogonal matrices $U$ of size $m \times m$ and $V$ of size
$n \times n$ and real numbers $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_n \ge 0$ with
$\sigma_j = 0$ for every $j > m$, such that $A = U \Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}$, where $\Sigma$ is the
$m \times n$ matrix with $\Sigma_{jj} = \sigma_j$ for $j \le \min(m, n)$ and all other entries
zero.

Proof: multiply the factorization $AV = U\Sigma$ on the right by $V^{\mathsf{T}}$.

articles.title: Singular value decomposition of a complex square matrix
articles.statement:
